newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: DOUBLED S.AFRICAN CLOTHING EXPORTS SEEN (RPT).
newsitem.headline: DOUBLED S.AFRICAN CLOTHING EXPORTS SEEN (RPT).

text.p: South Africa could double its clothing exports within two years if the government expedited export incentives promised in compensation for stringent tariff reductions, an industry leader said on Thursday.

Bernard Richards, chairman of the Clothing Federation of South Africa and managing director of Seardel Investment Corp , told reporters the government had failed to deliver on important industry reforms promised over a year ago.
He said supply-side measures promised by the then trade and industry minister Trevor Manuel, who is now finance minister, over a year ago had not been implemented.
"If we get the export incentives in place, we can kick our exports up from around 500 million rand a year to over a billion rand within a year or two," Richards said.
The measures, including an export marketing assistance programme, were promised to bolster the eight billion rand-a-year industry as protectionist import tariffs are cut.
"We believe that a fundamental economic mistake was made by government in that the tariff phase-down commenced in September 1995 ... without the supply-side measures in place.

"We have no finality at this point as to what these supply- side measures are. We have been running for 15 or 16 months with reduced tariffs and no supply-side measures and the result is that we have lost 15,000 jobs," he said.
The clothing industry, a mainstay of the Cape economy, employs around 170,000 people around the country.

Reporting on the outcome of the Clothing Federation's annual meeting and a meeting of a new Clothing and Textile Forum created to coordinate the interests of the two industries, Richards identified several areas of concern.
He said the government would be asked to extend conditions for preferential access to South African markets drafted for Zimbabwe to include neighbouring Malawi.
Malawi had become the second-biggest clothing exporter to South Africa after China, which bore no relationship to the size or capacity of the country's clothing industry.
"This tells you something is wrong," he said.

He said the clothing industry would seek an extension of a duty credit system in place for clothing made from local fabrics to cover clothing made on contract for outside clients who supplied materials.
The system of "outward processing" was the fastest growing phenomenon in the clothing industry, but South Africa had so far failed to win any business because of punitive duty laws.

Richards said that though textile industry representatives on the forum, which met for the first time on Wednesday, had not agreed to support the call, he believed it would eventually benefit local textile manufacturers as well.
"Once you have a foot in the door, things begin to develop. Everyone knows that," he said.
Richards said the industry was opposed to the restriction of a six-year tax holiday programme for new employment creation to new companies.
"If anyone has the capacity to create jobs, surely it is the existing industries," he said.
